summary.text: A covalent bond is a chemical bond in which atoms share electrons, forming electron pairs between them.
For many molecules, sharing lets each atom reach the equivalent of a full valence shell, which is a stable electronic configuration.
Sharing can be equal or unequal: atoms with equal electronegativity make nonpolar bonds, while unequal ones make polar bonds.

facts.label: Shared pairs
facts.value: The electron pairs are called shared pairs or bonding pairs

facts.label: Hydrogen sharing
facts.value: Hydrogen atoms share two electrons through covalent bonding

facts.label: Strongest type
facts.value: Sigma bonds are the strongest covalent bonds

facts.label: Double bond makeup
facts.value: One sigma bond and one pi bond

items.prompt: Two hydrogen atoms end up bonded together. What are the atoms doing with their electrons?

options.label: One atom hands its electron over and the two then cling by opposite charge
Each atom keeps its own electron and the nuclei simply attract each other
They share the two electrons, so a pair sits between the atoms
Both electrons are released and drift away from the pair of atoms

items.explain: The hydrogen atoms share the two electrons via covalent bonding. Handing an electron over would be ionic bonding instead.

items.prompt: Which pairing of atoms would make a bond with the most covalent character?

options.label: Two atoms that pull on electrons with similar strength
Two atoms where one pulls on electrons far harder than the other
Two atoms where one is far larger than the other
Two atoms that sit as far apart as the bond allows

items.explain: The covalent character of a bond is greatest between atoms with similar electronegativities, whether or not they are the same element.

items.prompt: In methane, one carbon atom bonds to four hydrogens. How many electrons surround the carbon in that arrangement?
items.explain: Carbon contributes four electrons and the four bonded hydrogens add four more, giving eight (the octet rule).

items.prompt: A chemist says two carbon atoms are joined by a double bond. What is that connection actually made of?

options.label: Two sigma bonds lying side by side
One sigma bond plus one pi bond
Two pi bonds with no sigma bond at all
One sigma bond plus two pi bonds

items.explain: A double bond consists of one sigma and one pi bond. A triple bond has one sigma and two pi bonds.

items.prompt: A molecule has bonds between unequal atoms, yet as a whole it is nonpolar. What could explain this?

options.label: Unequal atoms always share electrons equally once they are bonded
Its bonds must all be sigma bonds, which cannot be polar
Nonpolar molecules form only when the atoms pull with unequal strength
The pulls in different directions cancel out because of its geometry

items.explain: Polarity needs geometric asymmetry. In a symmetric molecule the dipoles can cancel, leaving a non-polar molecule.

items.prompt: Diamond, made of carbon atoms, does not melt until it gets extremely hot. What best explains this?

options.label: Huge numbers of its atoms are linked into one giant 3-dimensional network
Its small separate molecules are held together by weak forces
Its atoms are held together by electrostatic attraction between ions
Its atoms are barely connected, so heat is absorbed slowly

items.explain: Network covalent structures link large numbers of atoms in sheets or 3-dimensional structures like diamond, and such substances have high melting and boiling points.

beats.title: Sharing, not stealing
beats.hook: Some atoms bond with neither one winning the electrons.

beats.prompt: Two atoms with exactly equal electronegativity bond, as in H–H. How is the bonding pair shared?
beats.explain: Two atoms with equal electronegativity make nonpolar covalent bonds such as H–H; an unequal relationship creates a polar bond such as H−Cl.

choices.label: It is given entirely to one atom
choices.feedback: That would be an ionic picture. Here both atoms pull equally, so the pair is shared.

choices.label: Mostly held by one atom, giving a polar bond
choices.feedback: It tempts because bonds often look lopsided, but an unequal relationship only arises when the atoms differ in electronegativity.

choices.label: Equally, giving a nonpolar covalent bond

beats.prompt: Match each bond to how it is built.
beats.explain: Sigma bonds come from head-on overlap and pi bonds from lateral overlap, and multiple bonds stack pi bonds onto one sigma bond.

beats.prompt: Sort each covalent substance by how its atoms are arranged.
beats.explain: Individual molecules such as HCl, CO₂ and CH₄ are usually gases, while network structures link huge numbers of atoms in sheets or 3-dimensional arrangements, as in graphite, diamond and quartz.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about methane is wrong. Which?

steps.text: Carbon in methane has a valence of four.
Each of the four bonded hydrogens adds one electron to the carbon's count.
With carbon's own four, that puts eight electrons around carbon.
Each hydrogen likewise ends up surrounded by eight electrons.

beats.explain: Each hydrogen is surrounded by two electrons (its own plus one from carbon), following the duet rule, because its only shell holds just two.

beats.idea: Covalent bonds are shared electron pairs, and unequal pulls make the sharing lopsided.

paragraphs.heading: Sharing electrons
paragraphs.text: A covalent bond holds atoms together by having them share electrons, which form pairs between the atoms. These are called shared pairs or bonding pairs. Chemists use the name covalent bonding for the stable balance of pulling and pushing forces between atoms that share electrons. In many molecules, sharing lets each atom reach the equivalent of a full valence shell, the outer shell of electrons, which is a stable arrangement.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: Irving Langmuir introduced the term covalence in 1919, in an article in the Journal of the American Chemical Society. He used it for the number of electron pairs an atom shares with its neighbours. The prefix co- means jointly, so the word points to a valence that is shared. The idea is older than the name: in 1916 Gilbert N. Lewis had already described atoms sharing pairs of electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Lewis dots and the octet
paragraphs.text: Lewis introduced a notation that draws each atom's valence electrons, those in its outer shell, as dots around its symbol. A pair of dots between two atoms stands for a covalent bond, and several pairs stand for double or triple bonds. Lewis proposed that an atom forms as many covalent bonds as it needs to complete its outer shell. In methane, carbon has a valence of four and ends up surrounded by eight electrons, the octet rule. Each hydrogen ends up with two, following a duet rule.

paragraphs.heading: Sigma and pi bonds
paragraphs.text: The shared-pair picture is a good rough guide, but quantum mechanics is needed to explain these bonds and predict how simple molecules are built. Walter Heitler and Fritz London gave the first successful quantum explanation of a bond, in molecular hydrogen, in 1927. Their approach assumed that a bond forms when the atomic orbitals of the two atoms overlap well. Sigma bonds come from head-on overlap and are the strongest covalent bonds, while pi bonds come from sideways overlap and are weaker. A single bond is usually a sigma bond, a double bond is one sigma plus one pi, and a triple bond is one sigma plus two pi.

paragraphs.heading: Equal and unequal sharing
paragraphs.text: How polar a covalent bond is depends on the electronegativity of the two atoms. Two atoms with equal electronegativity make a nonpolar bond, as in H–H, while unequal ones make a polar bond, as in H−Cl. A molecule built from polar bonds can still be nonpolar overall if its shape is symmetric, because the bond dipoles cancel out. A bond is most covalent, and least ionic, when the atoms have similar electronegativities, whether or not they are the same element.

paragraphs.heading: From gases to diamonds
paragraphs.text: Covalent substances come in several kinds of structure. Separate small molecules with almost no pull between them, such as CO₂ and CH₄, are usually gases. Where molecules attract each other weakly, the result is a liquid that boils easily, like ethanol, or a solid that melts easily, like iodine. Long chains make polymers such as nylon, proteins and starch. Giant networks make graphite, diamond and quartz, which melt and boil only at high temperatures, are often brittle and tend to resist electric current.
